Schneider: </strong>Why is it so important for Chinese model makers to get famous in the US or achieve global adoption more broadly?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>Because I think there\u2019s a better ecosystem for developers and research still in the United States. You need to get accepted by the top researchers because if we don\u2019t open source our models, we\u2019ll never have an opportunity to join this conversation. It\u2019s important because we learn from X, from YouTube, from Reddit every day, and all the Chinese tech media are also paying attention to US KOLs or influencers.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider: </strong>This was very surprising, I think, to both Nathan and me \u2014 how recursive it was, where the Chinese media covers the Chinese models that the Americans are talking about. It\u2019s a very curious trend.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>Because you have people like Andrej Karpathy, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk. They not only talk about their own models but also what\u2019s going on elsewhere. Everyone knows \u2014 if they post a tweet, everyone knows what\u2019s going on, what models they\u2019re picking, what preferences they have, their views on maybe Qwen versus Codex. All the social media will try to grasp their core ideas immediately. That\u2019s very important. We also learned this from DeepSeek.</p><p>Frankly speaking, we used to neglect the importance of the global economy previously because we thought we needed to sell our products and APIs directly to Chinese enterprises. But nowadays, Chinese enterprises are still paying attention to the global brand and your global performance.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang: </strong>This reminded me of something I\u2019ve been curious about. We know the conversation is recursive. We know that Chinese tech pays a lot of attention to what Silicon Valley is looking at. But is there anything about the AI debate or discourse in China that Western media tends to miss? In your opinion, are there any issues or debates or things that people are really interested in that people in the English-speaking discourse tend to not understand?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>I just talked to a professor from Germany yesterday, and he mentioned some models that he knew people are talking about these days \u2014 Llama, Qwen, even Mistral \u2014 but not GLM. There are many people still unaware.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert: </strong>This person\u2019s a little out of date in the SF circles. More people are talking about GLM than Mistral and arguably Llama these days. You\u2019ve made a lot of progress.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>We\u2019ve made a lot of progress, but we track the discussion on Reddit and other social media, and we still see a lot of people asking what GLM is. Is it a good model? Where does it come from? It comes from nowhere or similar stuff. We still need to do a lot of things because we only have <a href=\\\"https://x.com/Zai_org\\\">20,000 followers on X</a>. People don\u2019t have a very deep understanding of GLM compared to other models.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert: </strong>I think DeepSeek has like a million. It\u2019s remarkable.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>Also, Mistral and Cohere get much more attention compared to Kimi and Z.ai. We still need to do better in our branding and our engagement in the technical community.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider: </strong>You mentioned selling API access to Chinese companies. Tell us a little bit about adoption in China. What\u2019s the sales process like? Do they all just have VPNs and use Claude? What\u2019s it like trying to do enterprise sales in China?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>You have two types of enterprises. One is companies that can\u2019t use APIs because they need to deploy the model on their own chips. They cannot accept sending data to other companies \u2014 not even to Z.ai or even Alibaba. That\u2019s a requirement for those companies. There are teams deploying DeepSeek for them \u2014 not from DeepSeek itself, but other companies can deploy DeepSeek for them. They usually build on top of the DeepSeek model with RAG, data storage, workflows, and other things.</p><p>The other type uses APIs \u2014 those are maybe tech companies and media companies. These companies accept APIs because they need to standardize their workflows. For API companies, they choose based on the balance between performance and price. ByteDance is doing great in that area. I believe ByteDance dominates the API services. Qwen is still trying to sell its APIs because Qwen 3 Max is a closed source version. If you\u2019ve heard of it, they have open sourced some models but also keep some things closed source for selling.</p><p>For us, we have open sourced our flagship models, so we are frequently asked, \u201CWhy is your service different from the open source version? Because we can deploy the open source version ourselves.\u201D We need a better engineering team, we need faster decoding speed. We need to do more on top of just having a good model. That might be our unique selling point. We need to do searches, we need to build our MCP. We\u2019re trying to get a competitive advantage over other GLM providers.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider: </strong>Is that annoying or fun?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>It\u2019s fun. It\u2019s fun because I think it\u2019s necessary to open source your models, so how you get a bite in that case is really important. We\u2019ve been figuring it out for a long time, but recently we found that subscription is a good idea \u2014 a GLM coding plan. With subscription, your users become more sticky. They love this area because you don\u2019t have to worry about how one prompt consumes tokens in your dialogue. Maybe inside Claude, a round of interaction will consume a million tokens, but you don\u2019t have to worry about it. We\u2019ll figure it out for our users.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert: </strong>Do you think you have meaningful adoption there? Because in the US market, I could start using Claude, Codex, Gemini, and whatever all for free with some basic Cursor. I was wondering \u2014 are people in the US actively using this? Is this a growing market that you think you\u2019re going to eat into? Qwen has one, and I might have tried it, but I\u2019m always like, \u201COh, I have my ChatGPT subscription.\u201D I\u2019m just wondering if, on the ground, it feels optimistic as something that is really shifting the needle.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>It\u2019s definitely very optimistic because we don\u2019t have to persuade 50% of people to do this \u2014 maybe you only need 5%. But 5% is a huge market. If 5% of Claude users shift their model to GLM, it\u2019s a huge market.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert: </strong>It\u2019s growing so fast, too.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li: </strong>But not just for Claude, because we\u2019re trying new ideas like role-playing. Many people on Silly Tavern are using GLM and Janitor AI because we do very well in role-playing. We\u2019re trying to have more markets \u2014 coding markets, chat markets. Maybe one day Meta will be using our model.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> All right, we\u2019ve got to take a step back and explain role playing. What is it? How do you make a model that\u2019s good at it? What are people using it for?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Before GLM-4.6, for models like GLM-4.5, we were relatively weak in role playing because we hadn\u2019t trained on that kind of data. We needed to create some data and let the model follow the instructions. For role playing, if you have a very long system prompt and you don\u2019t train on that kind of stuff, the model will forget who it is and forget all the instructions. It will just use its general performance to do the conversation. For a role-playing task, if given very long instructions, it must strictly follow those instructions and show more emotion or more specific behavior based on them.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> Just to be clear, this is people having a conversation, for example, saying, \u201CI\u2019m a Japanese pirate, I\u2019m raiding the coast of Taiwan in 1570, and I want to plan an attack to defend the fort.\u201D People write out like five pages of background.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We also tried something very interesting, like <em>Family Guy</em>. We have our own Stewie, and you just give a description of what the characher does and his history, and then you can create your own Stewie. We perform very well in text generation. If we had some speech model, we could recreate a Stewie there too.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> Was there a specific kind of pre-training data or RL that you needed to do to get this? How do you make a model that is really good at pretending to be cartoon characters?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> It\u2019s mainly post-training data.</p><h2>On AI Optimism and Translating Chinese Memes</h2><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> There\u2019s a big discussion of late in the US about people being worried that folks are falling in love with AI. There\u2019s this whole discussion about AI psychosis, where ChatGPT, for example, convinces people who trust it too much to harm themselves. I\u2019m curious about your broad sense of that type of discussion in China generally, and then internally in your firm, about the question of people using AI for emotional support.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> I just read a post from OpenAI yesterday. They invited a lot of experts to try and train a model that is not addictive. They trained data to ask ChatGPT to say it\u2019s an AI instead of saying it\u2019s a human being, not letting people get attached to ChatGPT anymore.</p><p>But from a broader audience perspective, not many people at Z.ai are looking into this yet because our model\u2019s capabilities are not there yet. If we had a model that could perform like GPT-5, then we could move on to removing the addiction.</p><p>Still, the performance is not on par with these top closed-source models, which we need to chase first. When we chase these models, we shift our focus to data collection and data preparation. Sometimes, the model behavior will change dramatically. If we do some similar things on our previous model, it will be outdated in the next version. Performance is still very relevant currently.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> I\u2019m guessing this is somewhere in the rundown, but what is the balance of optimism versus fear of AI as a long-term trajectory in your lab versus China generally? I think there\u2019s a very big concentration in the US of people who worry deeply about the long-term potential of AI, whether it\u2019s a powerful entity or a concentration of power or other things. Then there are people who just think this is the most important technology ever invented, and we have to be really serious about it. I\u2019m just wondering where on this spectrum you think the lab\u2019s culture is, or if it\u2019s not really something that\u2019s debated, and you\u2019re just focused on, \u201CWe\u2019re building a useful thing, and we\u2019re going to keep making it better.\u201D</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> I think developers fear the most. When you use code, when you use Codex, you get that fear in a very concrete way. It can do all the tasks for you, especially for junior developers. For writers or other managers, though, I think it\u2019s simpler because we already have SaaS and other technologies helping them. Large language models like ChatGPT are just another helper for them. So, I don\u2019t feel fear coming from the general public, but specifically for developers and data analysts. They fear the most because they try out the new models and new products more frequently than the general public, so they can feel the power.</p><p>Many people use DeepSeek and other chatbots. DeepSeek can help you brainstorm ideas, polish your writing, or do translation for you, but they don\u2019t believe that this work can replace them. But for developers, it\u2019s a different story.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> What are the main fears? Is it just people\u2019s jobs getting taken away? Or is it AI taking over the world? For the people who are worried, what exactly are they worried about?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Probably jobs being taken away.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Those fears are pretty different than in the US. There\u2019s definitely a huge culture \u2014 not a majority of the people, but a very vocal minority \u2014 that influences a lot of the thinking about the risks of AI well beyond just job loss. Job loss is almost an assumption for many people in the US, but there are added fears on top of this. I think that is a very different media ecosystem and thought ecosystem.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> I definitely know about this because I lived there. Obviously, everyone at MIT was talking about how AI will change the world, not on the positive side, but on the negative side.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> Why do you think this is? Is it that Chinese society is a little more practical, or is it just that job loss feels more imminent, or is it because it\u2019s less of a market-driven economy?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> I believe that people just know about DeepSeek. Maybe only 1 million people follow the latest trend, and a billion people do their work daily and are not impacted by AI. The more you learn about it, the more fear you have.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> What is the vibe among these younger engineers you\u2019re talking about? Specifically, the junior folks who are a little scared. I\u2019m generally curious what gets them into this work in the first place and what makes them want to work at places like Z.ai?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> At Z.ai, we lack people. There is no fear about losing jobs here because we have a lot of things to do. For other companies, especially large enterprises, they may have 10,000 people doing similar things, such as data analytics and back-end engineering work. They might think that if other people start using coding tools or agentic tools, maybe they only need 50% of their current staff.</p><p>They can do nothing, though. They need to wait for their bosses or the founders to make the decision, like what\u2019s happening at Amazon. For layoffs, you can do nothing \u2014 you just wait for the results.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> I\u2019d like to ask about translation because Z.ai\u2019s models are very strong in making very contextually rich translations from Chinese to English and deploying them onto social media. Could you talk a bit more about the process behind that, if you know? What is the secret sauce to translating memes?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We are doing very well in translation, especially the translation between Chinese and English. I think we are on par with Gemini 2.5 Pro. You mentioned memes \u2014 memes are one of our weapons because we prepared the data and understand the culture. We can even translate emojis. For example, if you enter a sentence talking about AI and you use a whale emoji to replace DeepSeek, we might translate this back to DeepSeek. However, if the sentence is actually about animals, we will translate the emoji into \u201Cwhale.\u201D We understand the context.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> Is this because Chinese internet talk is just so cryptic?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Yes, Chinese netizens are very novel. They sometimes use emojis. People also use abbreviations, so all those things need to be translated correctly.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> I remember a few years ago there was all this discussion that it was going to be really hard to train Chinese models to speak colloquially because all the data is behind walled gardens. For example, Tencent has the Tencent data, Xiaohongshu has the Xiaohongshu data, and Alibaba has its own data. Was that a problem for you guys doing this more colloquial, internet-speak work? Or is there enough out there that you can just scrape stuff and figure it out?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We need synthetic data. We do not have the actual data \u2014 we cannot scrape WeChat, but we know what people are talking about, especially in the public area. In the open area, we can observe what\u2019s going on on Xiaohongshu and on TikTok, for example. We especially pay attention to their comment area because people are very novel in their comments.</p><p>When the \u201CTikTok refugees\u201D situation happened, we actually benefited from it because more people and more software needed auto-translation. We are trying to conquer some large customers through our translation capabilities.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> Does anyone train on danmu \u5F39\u5E55 data [<em>Ed</em>. the rolling comments that appear on top of Bilibili videos]?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Definitely. We are trying to collect memes from everywhere, especially for our vision model, because memes are always in image format. We are trying to understand them with our vision model. I think it\u2019s very interesting and also very necessary because if you cannot translate the comment in a very accurate way, customers will not purchase your model.</p><p>It\u2019s unlike YouTube. If you use YouTube\u2019s auto-translation, it won\u2019t grasp the exact meaning. People just need to understand, \u201COh, this English version is about this, and I can read it in Chinese. 80% is enough for me.\u201D But for apps like X, Reddit, Xiaohongshu, or WeChat, you need to understand 100% of the comment area.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Is it a challenge to balance data across different cultures? Since you are marketing to Western users as well as having your domestic market, is that a technical challenge to feel like you have to do both excellently?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> It is a challenge. We can do very well in Chinese and English, and we are trying to explore more in French and even Hindi. We can perform very well in, I believe, about 20 languages. Beyond that, we are still exploring the data and the software. We need to register on their software to see what people are doing out there. Sometimes it\u2019s hard to figure out. We are trying to learn from Gemini and GPT-5 why they do so great in translation.</p><h2>Domestic Training and Hitting the Data Wall</h2><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> Do you guys train outside of China as well, or only on domestic clouds?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We do the inference outside China, but all the training is going on here.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> How do you feel about Huawei chips and software? Are they going to make it?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We are going to use them because we have multiple models, like GLM-4.6 and the upcoming 4.6 Air, as well as our previous version. We need to find the best use case for all sorts of chips: domestic chips and Nvidia chips. We need to classify the use case. One customer may need 30 tokens per second, and another customer may need 80 tokens per second. For one customer or one use case, some chips are enough, and for others, we need better chips and better inference techniques.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> Do you try to do any API sales or just enterprise sales in general outside the US or China?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We have two platforms. Inside China, our platform is called Big Model, which is a simple translation of \u201Clarge language model.\u201D It\u2019s BigModel.cn. We also have Z.ai, which is our overseas platform. I\u2019m actually in charge of API Z.ai. All of our services are hosted in Singapore. I\u2019m an employee of a Singaporean company.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> Do you see much demand for Z.ai coming from non-US countries, like other countries?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We see demand from a lot of countries \u2014 India, Indonesia, even Norway and Brazil. However, it depends on who\u2019s using Reddit and X, because we basically grew our user base on X, Reddit, and some on YouTube. We are trying to expand to platforms like Telegram, which might shift the proportion of our users. India and Indonesia are huge markets. More revenue, however, comes from the US compared to other countries because they pay more. They buy the Pro plan or Max plan instead of the Light plan. In terms of users, India has the most, but the US market generates 50% of our overseas revenue.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> Building off of what we were talking about earlier \u2014 that walled gardens didn\u2019t matter \u2014 does Z.ai have any thoughts about doing AI search on the Chinese Internet, and what that will look like in China, where there increasingly is no unified, open internet?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> That\u2019s a challenge for us product builders. Google doesn\u2019t have a search API, and Bing is trying to stop its search API. There are other third-party providers like SERP, which basically just scrape the data \u2014 they quickly send a request to Google and scrape the page. This is also very challenging for builders like Perplexity and even ChatGPT.</p><p>We need to rely on the technical side, nowadays using our own technology or trying to gather multiple resources from different platforms. That is very reasonable. There are other technologies, like manuscript, that just browse the Internet themselves without using an API. That\u2019s more doable these days. When you want to see multiple resources and try to distinguish the best use case or the best resources, you need to really log into an account and see the data yourself, read the page yourself, instead of just using whatever API gives you.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Where are you planning to take your models next?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Right now, we are exploring on-policy training and on-policy reinforcement learning. We are quite mature in off-policy reinforcement learning, but for on-policy learning, we still need to explore more. Also, multi-agents.</p><p>When you look at Z.ai chat, it actually acts like a single agent. One model does the search, comes back, does another round of search, then comes back, and it can generate slides, a presentation, or a poster, things like that. But it\u2019s all performed by a single actor, the one GLM-4.6</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Do we think we have to change our models a lot in order to do this? So much of 2025 has been changing the training stack away from \u201Cwe are a chatbot\u201D to \u201Cwe are an agent.\u201D What do you think we should change the most about our models, given that the faster model, like the Air model, might be more useful because you can have more of them?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> That\u2019s the reason why we need to do a very solid evaluation because we have different product solutions. Currently, the single agent works very well on our platform. We need to do more to try out different ideas and see whether we can improve the speed and performance with a multi-agent architecture and other possibilities. For single agents, it has better context management because you have the best model that can see all the context ahead of the current conversation and follow the instructions up to that point. For multi-agents, however, you need to compress the context for each agent, and that might lose some context or information.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Or the orchestration is hard. If you give four agents the same context, they might all try the same thing, and they might not work together well.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Yes. If even one agent has a hallucination, it will ruin all the research. We are also trying to make a longer context window and a longer effective context window. We all know that you can say your model can do a one-million context window, but it actually performs very well only inside 60k or maybe 100k.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> You can release whatever size of context model you want, but the question is whether or not it actually works.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Exactly.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> How much do you think it\u2019s going to be scaling the kind of transformers that we have \u2014 making the long context better, just improving the data \u2014 versus if there are fundamental walls that this is approaching? It\u2019s kind of the low-hanging fruit question. Do you just think there\u2019s a ton to keep improving, or is it kind of easy to find the things to do, and you just don\u2019t have time?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> It\u2019s not easy. We believe it\u2019s the architecture thing. Data can improve performance, but it cannot cross the wall. There is a wall. We need a better architecture, better pre-training data, and better post-training data.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Do you think you\u2019re starting to hit this wall, or do you kind of see it coming already? Is this something you\u2019re forecasting, or are you seeing, \u201COh, this specific thing \u2014 data alone is not solving it for us\u201D? People in the US who are training these models just don\u2019t talk about it; they say, \u201CI can\u2019t say.\u201D I\u2019m curious. The models I train are smaller \u2014 I think our biggest model is about 30 billion scale. When you scale up, you start to see very different limits to what\u2019s happening.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We need to do some experiments. GLM is a 355-billion-parameter model, but we cannot do experiments with this large model. We need to do experiments with some smaller models, maybe 9 billion or 30 billion parameters, and test our hypothesis. Ninety percent of the time, we just fail, because you cannot win every time with experiments. You need to do a lot of scientific work to finally get the right answer.</p><p>If you are talking about whether the GLM-4.6 architecture will hit the wall, there is actually a wall. We need to shift our focus and start from maybe a new architecture or a new framework for doing this stuff.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> It sounds like these bigger runs were not necessarily barely making it, but definitely stressful for you.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Yes, it\u2019s stressful. We are going to use some engineering solutions to try to compress the text windows to make our users happy. You don\u2019t normally need one million tokens yet. If it cannot perform very well, you can compress the context window to 60k or 30k to make it work.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> You mentioned earlier that all the inference is abroad, but training is at home. What\u2019s the rationale behind that decision?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> The rationale is very simple \u2014 we provide services to overseas customers. I think it\u2019s a requirement to store the data overseas. That is a very strict policy for our Z.ai endpoint. We change that privacy policy every month to make it stricter and more coherent with people\u2019s expectations.</p><p>For the training, I think it\u2019s simpler because we don\u2019t have many resources. We only have these resources, and we need to utilize them.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> But doing it on Azure or AWS in Malaysia or Singapore \u2014 is that too expensive, or too slow? Do you guys already have enough chips at home? What\u2019s the thinking there?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> I don\u2019t think it\u2019s very slow \u2014 it\u2019s fast because we change the location of not only the GPU but also the CPU and the database. If they are all in Singapore, it is still very fast. If you have to go back from Singapore to mainland China and then go back to Singapore, it will be slow.</p><p>On the training side, I think it\u2019s very simple. We\u2019re not OpenAI or Anthropic; we don\u2019t have to choose between Amazon and Google and their own infrastructure. They are doing very complicated things. For us, I think we are still in the initial stage. We don\u2019t have many complicated structures with these large inference providers, so things are still simple here.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> For now.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> For now, yes.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> Irene or Nathan, any more training questions before we wrap up?</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Only sensitive questions that I don\u2019t expect to have an answer to: How big is your next model? How many GPUs do you have?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> For our next generation, we are going to launch 4.6 Air. I don\u2019t know whether it will be called Mini, but it is a 30-billion-parameter model. It becomes a lot smaller in a couple of weeks. That\u2019s all for 2025.</p><p>For 2026, we are still doing experiments, like what I said, trying to explore more. We are doing these experiments on smaller models, so they will not be put into practice in 2026. However, it gives us a lot of ideas on how we are going to train the next generation. We will see. When this podcast launches, I believe we already have 4.6 Air, 4.6 Mini, and also the next 4.6 Vision model.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> A good question is: How long does it take from when the model is done training until you release it? What is your thought process on getting it out fast versus carefully validating it?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Get it out fast. We open source it within a few hours.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> I love it.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> When we finish the training, we do some evaluation, and after the evaluation, we just release it. We don\u2019t send the endpoint to LM Arena or to other analysis companies to let them evaluate it first and then release the model. We don\u2019t have that. We also don\u2019t have a \u201Cnano banana\u201D thing to try and make it famous before it\u2019s launched because we are very transparent. We believe that if you want to open source the model, the open source itself is the biggest event.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> Do you try to time the release with a market event or anything?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We are trying to do some marketing from my side, and I want to make the rollout longer. I want a week for me to collaborate with inference providers, benchmark companies, and coding agents, and let everyone trial the model before it\u2019s released.</p><p>From the company\u2019s perspective, if open source is the most important thing, you only need to prepare the materials for the open source itself. You need the benchmarks and maybe a tech blog. It is very stressful for me because I need to negotiate with multiple partners within several hours. \u201CWe have a new model coming in two hours, maybe three hours. Maybe you are sleeping, but this is huge.\u201D We don\u2019t give enough time for people to connect to the model or do the integration, but we\u2019re trying to post your tweet afterwards.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> Now, in America, we have our own thing, 002.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> What is 002?</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> Midnight to midnight with a two-hour break. It\u2019s so dumb.</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Hours vary a lot, even inside the company. Someone might leave the company at 7 p.m., while someone else will never leave the company. For me, I work 18 hours a day because I need to negotiate with US large firm CEOs or the founders of coding agents. I need to discuss with Fireworks, with LM Arena, and with Kilo Code CEOs. I have to follow their time and do meetings, sometimes at 2 a.m. or 3 a.m. That\u2019s all possible.</p><p>For our researchers or the engineering team, your brains can only work maybe eight hours a day. If you feel tired, you need to get some rest. It\u2019s impossible to ask a top researcher to work 24 hours a day. That would mean you are either working inefficiently or you are just attending meetings. But if you want to read papers, do experiments, and write code, eight hours is enough.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> That\u2019s very sensible.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> My PhD advisor always said that you can completely change the world if you do four hours a day of top technical work. Just go walk in the sun after that \u2014 you did a good job.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> How do you explain the value of your work to, let\u2019s say, high school kids in Beijing? Or your grandmother?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> It\u2019s hard. I can only say I do something similar to DeepSeek. Everyone in high school, and even in kindergarten, knows about DeepSeek.</p><p>For developers, it\u2019s simple: we are one of the best coding LLMs you can find, especially in China. But for high school students, they always ask, \u201CWe have DeepSeek, what are you doing? Why do we need you? Are you doing a similar thing, or are you better? Are you faster?\u201D That\u2019s very tough.</p><p>We still need to improve the model performance. That\u2019s the top priority. Product experience is the second. Without a solid model, nobody will pay attention to you. If we are at the same level, only the most famous one gets all the attention.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> So you think the salience of AI models, generalized across society, came straight out of DeepSeek and the kind of nationalism associated with that?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> There is a hype. They got so famous, even in China, so we are unknown even here. I believe a lot of students in Tsinghua University haven\u2019t tried GLM or haven\u2019t even heard of this company. Everybody knows the famous names, but not everyone goes to this building to visit Z.ai, right? DeepSeek is all over the news and social media, so it\u2019s really tough to explain our contribution and our value.</p><p><strong>Irene Zhang:</strong> Do you think Chinese society is starting to find AI to be more valuable, or is it getting scarier than valuable?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> We are not there yet. AI is not so strong as to make people fear it because there is still hallucination, and it\u2019s still not always following instructions. There are still a lot of issues to solve before it becomes more fearful or terrifying for people.</p><p><strong>Jordan Schneider:</strong> We end every episode with a song. Does Zhipu have a theme song, or what do people listen to when they code around the office?</p><p><strong>Zixuan Li:</strong> Actually, no. Our founder loves running, but music not so much. He is a pro in the marathon. The founder of Moonshot really loves music, but our founder doesn\u2019t have much interest in it. For our anniversary, we have a half-marathon to celebrate.</p><p><strong>Nathan Lambert:</strong> I\u2019ve got to go do this. I\u2019m going to go run the Z.ai half-marathon next year.</p><p><em>Correction: A section of this transcription originally recorded Zixuan as saying, \u201CIn 2025, with the launch of Moonshot\u2019s Kimi Chat (Kimi K2 model), we realized that coding and agentic functions are more useful.\u201D It is, in fact, \u201CIn 2025, with the launch of Manus and Claude Code, we realized that coding and agentic functions are more useful.\u201D The transcript has been updated</em></p><div class=\\\"subscription-widget-wrap-editor\\\" data-attrs=\\\"{"url":"https://www.chinatalk.media/subscribe?","text":"Subscribe","language":"en"}\\\" data-component-name=\\\"SubscribeWidgetToDOM\\\"><div class=\\\"subscription-widget show-subscribe\\\"><div class=\\\"preamble\\\"><p class=\\\"cta-caption\\\">ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication.
